Subfactors, index and finite-depth classification

Reflection, commuting squares and finite depth

A finite-index inclusion has an infinite Jones tower, but each higher relative commutant is finite dimensional. The Jones projection identifies an old part at the next level by reflection. Whatever remains records new information. Finite depth means that, from some point onward, no new part appears.

We assume Going up and down the Jones tower, Measuring an inclusion through modules and corners, Finite bases, bounded vectors and a positive-operator inequality, Matrix inclusions and the Markov trace, and Positivity restricts the index. References are [Jones] and [Popa].

Theorems 12.5–12.7 prove support persistence, graph norm and the discrete depth bound; Proposition 12.8 retains the general pointwise graph-weight equation. The explicit level corrections and Example 12.9 are the comparison with Takesaki, Chapter XIX, §4.

The traces, inclusions and Jones projections belong to this data. Forgetting them and retaining only the sizes of the matrix blocks loses information. We call this structured ladder the standard invariant in its higher-relative-commutant form.

The inclusion has finite depth if such a exists. We use the convention

Otherwise the depth is infinite. With this convention the identity inclusion has depth one.

The principal graph is the rooted bipartite graph obtained from the tower of inclusion diagrams by keeping the initial root , introducing a new vertex for each matrix summand in a new part, and identifying the old summands by the basic-construction bijection in (12.6). Edges have the inclusion multiplicities. The transpose rule means that the old edges are reproduced in reverse at the next step, rather than introducing new edges or vertices.

There is a useful further restriction on the new edges. For , the projections and are equivalent in . Thus annihilates both, and consequently annihilates the old ideal in . A new block of can receive edges only from the new blocks of . It cannot introduce an extra edge from an older vertex. This proves, inductively, that a newly introduced vertex has distance from the root. The level- summands therefore correspond to the graph vertices reachable from the root in steps, and their block sizes are the numbers of such walks. The initial embedding of scalars gives the starting edge multiplicities; counting extensions gives the induction step.

Every new vertex is connected to an earlier one, because the inclusions are unital. The graph is therefore connected. Theorem 12.5 shows that finite depth is equivalent to the appearance of only finitely many vertices. In that case, after all vertices are reached, the inclusion matrices alternate between the two orientations of the full bipartite adjacency matrix. The dual principal graph is obtained in the same way from , whose relative-commutant tower is .

Index below four forces finite depth

Theorem 12.7. If , where , then

Proof. The Jones–Wenzl projection for the first Jones projections has trace zero and is zero, by Theorem 7.2 and faithfulness. This projection is the largest projection annihilated by all those generators. To check maximality, induct through its recursion: any projection annihilating the preceding generators lies below ; if it also annihilates the next generator, multiplication by the next recursion leaves it unchanged, so it lies below . The recursion itself annihilates each generator, giving equality with the joint-kernel projection.

Hence

Thus the listed projections have the same central support there; their join being one forces that support to be one. In particular has full central support in . Definition (12.7) gives depth at most . For , the single projection is , giving depth one.

Finite depth controls this finite-dimensional structure. Reconstructing a hyperfinite inclusion from the full ladder requires a generating tunnel; graph norm and block multiplicities alone do not prove that classification theorem.
